title: Hardin Village (15Gp22)
summary: In Greenup County, Hardin Village was a late Fort Ancient farming town of large houses, occupied from the late 1500s to the mid-1600s.
bodyMarkdown:
Hardin Village is a late Fort Ancient town in Greenup County. It was one of the last large Native farming villages in the region before European explorers arrived. Excavations have made it a key site for understanding Fort Ancient homes, trade and health.

## Dating the village

The sources differ on when people lived there. The [Kentucky Archaeological Survey's Hardin page](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Hardin.aspx) dates the village from the late 1500s to the mid-1600s. Another account [places it](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardin_Village_site) in the Montour phase, settled in the early 1500s and abandoned by about 1625. Both agree it was gone before French and English explorers reached the area.

The archaeology survey says the village covered more than 10 acres. It was surrounded by a defensive palisade like other Fort Ancient villages. Unlike most of them, it seems to have had no central oval plaza, and houses stood in clusters.

## Houses

The survey says the University of Kentucky excavated Hardin in 1939 and again in the early 2010s, finding eight houses with storage pits, hearths and trash pits. Digs took place in the late 1930s, 1966 and 2015.

The houses were large, from 51 to 70 feet long and 24 to 29 feet wide. Each wall post was set in its own hole, and with no sign of daub, the walls were probably covered with bark. The size suggests that two or more related families shared each house, cooking at central hearths.

## Burials and health

Families buried their dead in cemeteries close to the houses. Hearths near the cemeteries suggest feasts were part of funerals, as at other Fort Ancient villages. Most people were laid on their backs in an extended position. The site held 301 to 445 burials, the most found at any Fort Ancient site in Kentucky.

Bone chemistry shows that corn was central to the diet, along with beans and squash grown in nearby fields. The sugary corn diet led to many cavities. Infant mortality was high, but the survey notes that a child who lived past two had a good chance of reaching adulthood.

## Trade

Hardin's people obtained marine shell beads and brass objects from their neighbors. These exotic goods came by way of Mississippian peoples to the south and west. What the villagers offered in return is not known. Large numbers of triangular endscrapers, used to clean hides, suggest they may have traded animal skins.

About three-quarters of the pottery is of the type called Madisonville-Fox Farm Cordmarked. The potters tempered clay with ground mussel shell, a Mississippian technique.

## Kentucky today

Hardin Village is a protected archaeological site, so its location is given here only as Greenup County. The village was home to Native families for generations and deserves respect.
